n: Ireland — Mother and Baby Homes Commission: 9,000 child deaths; adoptions abroad
who: Religious orders (incl. Bon Secours Sisters), local authorities and the Irish state
d: The Commission of Investigation's final report (published 12 January 2021) covered 14 mother and baby homes and 4 county homes. About 9,000 children died in them between 1922 and 1998, about one in seven births and about twice the general infant mortality rate. Several homes had been linked to illegal domestic and foreign adoptions, many to the United States. On 13 January 2021 Taoiseach Micheál Martin apologised for a 'profound generational wrong'. (The care agent may hold the home-conditions record; this record focuses on removals and adoptions.)
cover: In May 2018 Tusla referred 126 cases of births falsely registered by the St Patrick's Guild adoption agency (illegal registrations that hid children's identities).
cite: Mother and Baby Homes Commission of Investigation, Final Report, 12 January 2021, as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Australia — forced adoptions: Senate inquiry 2012 and national apology 2013
who: Australian governments, hospitals, churches and adoption agencies
d: From the 1950s to the 1980s babies of unmarried mothers were taken for adoption, often without informed consent. The Senate Community Affairs References Committee reported on 29 February 2012 ('Commonwealth Contribution to Former Forced Adoption Policies and Practices'). Prime Minister Julia Gillard delivered a national apology on 21 March 2013, after state apologies starting with Western Australia (19 October 2010), South Australia, ACT, NSW and Victoria in 2012.
cite: Senate Community Affairs References Committee report, 29 Feb 2012; National Apology for Forced Adoptions, 21 March 2013 (via Wikipedia 'Forced adoption in Australia')

n: Australia — Stolen Generations: Bringing Them Home (1997) and national apology (2008)
who: Australian federal, state and territory governments; church and state missions and institutions
d: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children were forcibly removed from their families under government policies roughly between 1910 and 1970 and placed in institutions, missions, foster or adoptive families. The Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission's 1997 report 'Bringing Them Home' found that between one in three and one in ten children were separated in some regions. Prime Minister Kevin Rudd apologised on 13 February 2008. Redress schemes followed: Tasmania (2006, A$5m), NSW (2017, A$75,000 per survivor) and a A$378m Commonwealth scheme for NT, ACT and Jervis Bay (announced 6 August 2021).
cite: HREOC, Bringing Them Home, 1997; Wikipedia 'Stolen Generations'

n: Canada — Sixties Scoop: Ontario ruling 2017 and C$800m settlement
who: Federal government of Canada and provincial child welfare authorities
d: From the late 1950s into the 1980s about 20,000 Indigenous children were taken from their families and fostered or adopted, mostly into white middle-class families, some in the United States. On 14 February 2017 Justice Edward Belobaba of the Ontario Superior Court (Brown v. Canada, 2017 ONSC 251) found Canada breached its duty of care to prevent on-reserve children in Ontario from losing their Aboriginal identity. On 6 October 2017 an C$800 million settlement was announced, paying C$25,000–50,000 per eligible status First Nations or Inuit former ward, plus a C$50m healing foundation.
cite: Brown v. Canada (Attorney General), 2017 ONSC 251; settlement announced 6 October 2017 (via Wikipedia 'Sixties Scoop')

n: United States — Indian Adoption Project (1958–67) and the Indian Child Welfare Act 1978
who: Bureau of Indian Affairs, US Children's Bureau, Child Welfare League of America
d: The Indian Adoption Project placed 395 Native American children with white families between 1958 and 1967. Congress passed the Indian Child Welfare Act in 1978 after hearings described the 'wholesale separation of Indian children from their families'. In June 2001 the Child Welfare League of America's executive director said the project was 'wrong' and 'hurtful'.
cite: Wikipedia 'Indian Adoption Project' citing H.R. Rep. 95-1386 (1978) and CWLA statement, June 2001

n: Israel — Yemenite, Mizrahi and Balkan children affair
who: Israeli state health and immigration institutions
d: Families, mostly Yemenite immigrants, said babies taken to hospitals in 1948–1954 disappeared and were told they had died. Three state inquiries (1967, 1988, 2001) concluded most had died; the 2001 Kedmi commission examined over 800 cases, finding 750 deaths and 56 unresolved, and the 1967 committee found 2 adoptions. About 400,000 documents were released on 28 December 2016. In February 2021 the government expressed sorrow and approved compensation of up to NIS 200,000 per family whose child's fate is unknown.
cite: Wikipedia 'Yemenite Children Affair' (citing Haaretz, Times of Israel, BBC)

n: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial)
who: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA), Lebensborn e.V., SS
d: Nazi Germany seized children judged 'racially valuable' in occupied Poland and elsewhere, held them in Lebensborn or health-department camps and placed them with German families under new identities. The RuSHA trial (United States v. Ulrich Greifelt et al., eighth of the 12 Nuremberg follow-up trials, 10 October 1947 – 10 March 1948) ruled that the abductions and Germanization were part of genocide. Heinemann's research identified 20,000 Polish children who passed Germanization criteria; about 1,000 were taken from Bohemia and Moravia and 1,100 from Slovenia.
cite: Nuremberg Military Tribunal, RuSHA case, judgment 10 March 1948; Wikipedia 'Kidnapping of children by Nazi Germany'

n: France — Children of Creuse: 2,015 Réunionese children moved to mainland France
who: French state social services (DDASS); scheme led by Réunion MP Michel Debré
d: Between 1963 and 1982 the French state declared Réunionese children wards of the state, often after parents signed abandonment papers they could not read, and moved them to depopulating rural departments of mainland France. Some were adopted; others stayed in homes or worked unpaid on farms. The newspaper Témoignages denounced 'child trafficking' in August 1968. In 2014 the National Assembly passed a resolution recognising the state failed its 'moral responsibility' to the children.
cite: French National Assembly resolution, 18 February 2014 (via Wikipedia 'Children of Creuse')

n: United States — Georgia Tann / Tennessee Children's Home Society black-market adoptions
who: Tennessee Children's Home Society (Shelby County branch) under Georgia Tann
d: From 1924 to 1950 Georgia Tann used the Memphis branch of the Tennessee Children's Home Society to take children from poor families and sell them, charging up to $5,000 for out-of-state adoptions when Tennessee adoptions cost about $7. A state investigation into adoption fraud led to the home's closure in 1950; Tann died before its findings were published.
cite: Tennessee State Library and Archives, Georgia Tann/Tennessee Children's Home Society Investigation Scrapbooks, 1950 (via Wikipedia 'Georgia Tann')

n: Russia — Dima Yakovlev Law bans adoption by US citizens
who: Russian state
d: Federal Law 272-FZ, signed by President Putin on 28 December 2012 and effective 1 January 2013, banned US citizens from adopting Russian children. It was named after Dima Yakovlev, a Russian toddler who died in July 2008 after his adoptive father left him in a car in Virginia, and was widely seen as retaliation for the US Magnitsky Act. In April 2010 a US adoptive mother had sent her 7-year-old adopted son alone on a flight back to Moscow, prompting Russian calls for a suspension. (This is a closure event, not a trafficking finding.)
cite: Kremlin.ru, 28 December 2012; Federal Law 272-FZ (via Wikipedia 'Dima Yakovlev Law')

n: Haiti — New Life Children's Refuge: US missionaries try to take 33 children after earthquake
who: New Life Children's Refuge (Idaho Baptist missionaries) led by Laura Silsby
d: On 29 January 2010, after the earthquake, ten American Baptist missionaries were arrested trying to take 33 children across the Dominican border without authorisation; SOS Children's Villages reported most, if not all, were not orphans. They were charged on 4 February 2010 with kidnapping and criminal association; nine were released. On 17 May 2010 leader Laura Silsby was convicted of arranging irregular travel and sentenced to time served.
cite: CNN, 5 February 2010; BBC, 5 February 2010 (via Wikipedia 'New Life Children's Refuge case')

n: Vietnam — Operation Babylift (1975): not all children were orphans
who: US government (Military Airlift Command); Holt International, Friends of Children of Viet Nam, Friends For All Children and other agencies
d: In April 1975 the US airlifted over 3,300 infants and children out of South Vietnam; the first flight, on 4 April, crashed killing 78 children. A lawsuit filed on 29 April 1975 on behalf of the Committee to Protect the Rights of Vietnamese Children alleged that many children were not orphans and were taken without parents' consent; many had been placed in orphanages by living relatives.
cite: New York Times, 1 May 1975; USAID Operation Babylift Report 1975 (via Wikipedia 'Operation Babylift')

n: El Salvador — children disappeared by the armed forces during the civil war (Pro-Búsqueda)
who: Salvadoran armed forces
d: Pro-Búsqueda, founded in 1994, has documented close to a thousand children disappeared during the Salvadoran civil war, mostly by the armed forces; many were adopted through flawed procedures to the US, France, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands. On 1 March 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled on the 1982 disappearance of the Serrano Cruz sisters during the 'Guinda de Mayo' military operation. El Salvador created a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children in 2010.
cover: The armed forces have not granted access to archives on disappeared children despite years of lobbying.
cite: Inter-American Court of Human Rights, Serrano-Cruz Sisters v. El Salvador, 1 March 2005; Wikipedia 'Pro-Búsqueda'

n: Spain — children of Republican prisoners taken by the Franco regime
who: Franco regime; Auxilio Social; Women's Protection Board (Patronato de Protección a la Mujer); Falange
d: A 1940 law allowed imprisoned mothers to keep children only until age three, after which the state took custody; 12,043 Republican children were in state custody in 1943. In 2008 Judge Baltasar Garzón characterised the removals as crimes against humanity and said the Falange was involved in kidnapping or forcibly repatriating children and changing their names. In January 2011 families of 261 babies who disappeared from hospitals over about fifty years took their cases to the attorney general; lawyers' estimates of up to 300,000 were rejected by a 2026 forensic study, which did not dispute about 30,000 children placed in state care.
cover: Names were changed so children could be given to pro-regime families; the 1977 Amnesty Law has hindered investigation, and many Women's Protection Board files went missing in 1996.
cite: Audiencia Nacional, Garzón ruling (El País, 2008); Wikipedia 'Lost children of Francoism'

n: Chad — Zoé's Ark tries to fly 103 children to France (convicted 2007)
who: French charity L'Arche de Zoé (founder Éric Breteau)
d: On 30 October 2007 six members of the French charity Zoé's Ark were charged in Chad with abducting 103 children they said were Darfur orphans to be fostered in France; most were found to be Chadian with at least one living parent or guardian. The six were convicted on 26 December 2007 and sentenced to eight years' forced labour (to be served in France) and ordered to pay restitution to each of the 103 children; a Chadian and a Sudanese national got four years, and two Chadian officials were acquitted. Chad's president pardoned the six in March 2008.
cite: BBC News, 29 October 2007; Wikipedia 'Zoé's Ark'

n: Canada — Ideal Maternity Home ('Butterbox Babies'), Nova Scotia
who: William Peach Young and Lila Gladys Young
d: The unlicensed Ideal Maternity Home charged unmarried mothers $500 and sold babies on the black market for up to $10,000, including across borders. The Nova Scotia Department of Public Welfare gathered evidence from 1934; the Youngs were convicted of fraud in 1935, acquitted of manslaughter in 1936, and convicted in 1946 on seven violations of the Maternity Boarding Houses Act before the home was shut. A 1946 Montreal Standard article called them international traffickers in babies.
cite: Wikipedia 'Ideal Maternity Home' (citing Bette Cahill, Butterbox Babies, 1992)

n: Denmark — 1951 'little Danes' experiment: 22 Greenlandic children removed
who: Danish government, Danish Red Cross, Save the Children Denmark
d: In May 1951 Danish authorities, with the Red Cross and Save the Children, sent 22 Greenlandic Inuit children to Danish foster families to re-educate them as 'little Danes'; they were supposed to be orphans but only six were. Six were adopted in Denmark and 16 returned to a Danish-speaking orphanage in Greenland and never lived with their families again. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen apologised in December 2020, and in March 2022 the six survivors were awarded 250,000 kroner each.
cite: BBC News, 9 March 2022; KNR, 28 February 2022 (via Wikipedia 'Little Danes experiment')

n: Switzerland — authorities' irregularities in intercountry adoptions (Sri Lanka, India, Tibet…); proposed ban
who: Swiss federal and cantonal authorities; private adoption agencies
d: Swiss authorities knew that children placed for adoption, often wrongly presented as orphans, were linked to economic interests and organised child trafficking, yet decisions were made on incomplete or falsified documents and parental consent was not checked. After a 2018 parliamentary mandate for a study, the Federal Council acknowledged the authorities' irregularities and omissions in 2020 and 2023, and in late 2024 advocated a general ban on intercountry adoption. AP reported Switzerland 'apologized for failing to prevent illegal adoptions'.
cite: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland, 'Adoption' (Urs Germann, 2025) via Wikipedia 'Adoption in Switzerland'; AP/PBS Frontline, 20 September 2024

n: Switzerland — 'Kinder der Landstrasse': Yenish children removed by Pro Juventute (1926–1973)
who: Pro Juventute foundation, with federal and cantonal authorities
d: From 1926 to 1973 the Pro Juventute 'Hilfswerk für die Kinder der Landstrasse', backed by federal authorities, removed about 590 Yenish children from their families and placed them in foster homes, orphanages, psychiatric hospitals and prisons, with contact with parents systematically prevented. It ended after the Beobachter exposé of 15 April 1972. Victims later received a total of 11 million francs. In February 2025 the Swiss government acknowledged the persecution as a crime against humanity, following a September 2024 legal opinion. (Care agent covers Verdingkinder.)
cite: Swiss Federal Archives study (1998); Federal Council summary of the Diggelmann/Emery/Rüfli opinion, 2025

n: United States — 'Baby Scoop Era' adoptions of unmarried mothers' babies (1945–1973)
who: Maternity homes, adoption agencies, social workers
d: From 1945 to 1973 up to 4 million US parents, mostly unmarried mothers, had children placed for adoption, often presented as the only option with little effort to help mothers keep their babies. Non-relative adoptions rose from about 33,800 in 1951 to 89,200 in 1970. No national official inquiry has been held (unlike Australia, Ireland and the UK).
cite: The Adoption History Project (University of Oregon), 'Adoption Statistics'; Wikipedia 'Baby Scoop Era'

n: United States / UK — 'internet twins' sold twice through an online adoption broker
who: Internet agency A Caring Heart (broker in California)
d: In 2000–01 twin baby girls were placed through the online agency A Caring Heart first with a California couple and then with a couple from Wales who paid about £8,200; police in Wales took the twins into care in January 2001 and on 9 April 2001 the High Court ordered them returned to the US. The FBI raided the agency in March 2001; the broker was charged with wire fraud in 2003 but charges were dropped in 2005 for insufficient evidence. The case led to UK adoption reform.
cite: The Guardian, 'The internet twins: timeline', 9 April 2001; CBS News, 14 March 2001 (via Wikipedia)

n: MINUSTAH Sri Lankan contingent — child sexual exploitation ring, Haiti
who: Sri Lanka Army contingent of the UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti (MINUSTAH)
d: In November 2007, 114 members of the 950-strong Sri Lankan contingent were accused of sexual misconduct and abuse, and 108, including three officers, were sent home. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services concluded that 'acts of sexual exploitation and abuse (against children) were frequent and occurred usually at night, and at virtually every location where the contingent personnel were deployed', and said charges should include statutory rape. An Associated Press investigation in April 2017 found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had exploited at least nine children in a sex ring between 2004 and 2007; none was jailed.
cover: Repatriation instead of prosecution: 114 members accused in November 2007 and 108 (incl. 3 officers) sent home; Sri Lankan authorities judged the acts 'consensual' and nobody was jailed.
cite: Wikipedia 'MINUSTAH' and 'Sexual abuse scandal in Haiti' (citing OIOS findings and AP, 12 April 2017)

n: French Operation Sangaris soldiers — alleged abuse of children, Bangui
who: French army, Operation Sangaris (not under UN command)
d: A confidential report commissioned by the UN human rights office, made public by The Guardian on 29 April 2015, recorded accounts that 16 French soldiers had sexually abused at least about ten children in Bangui between December 2013 and June 2014, including boys aged 9 to 13 in exchange for food or money near the airport camp. French investigating judges issued a dismissal (non-lieu) on 11 January 2018 for insufficient charges; the Paris prosecutor said it 'cannot be affirmed at the end of the investigation that no sexual abuse was committed'. No soldier was charged. CAR authorities said they deplored the decision.
cover: The internal UN report was not passed to French authorities by the UN; the UN official who passed it on (Anders Kompass) was suspended and resigned in 2016 in protest at impunity.
cite: French Wikipedia 'Opération Sangaris' (citing The Guardian 29 Apr 2015, AFP, decision of 11 Jan 2018)

n: MINUSCA — DR Congo battalion repatriated after child abuse allegations
who: Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) battalion serving with MINUSCA
d: An 807-strong FARDC battalion deployed to MINUSCA in 2015 faced allegations including child sexual exploitation and abuse; in January 2016 the UN announced it would be repatriated, citing failure to meet vetting and preparedness requirements. The 2016 UN data list 17 allegations involving DRC military personnel in MINUSCA with 15 child victims.
cite: Wikipedia 'MINUSCA'; UN doc A/71/818 annex tables (2016 allegations)

n: UNTAC Cambodia — growth of prostitution around peacekeepers
who: UN Transitional Authority in Cambodia (UNTAC) personnel (about 15,900 military)
d: The arrival of UNTAC's roughly 22,000 personnel was followed by a sharp rise in prostitution, from an estimated 6,000 to more than 25,000 sex workers in two years, and by abuse of Cambodian women and girls; the UN did not keep thorough records of allegations at the time, so numbers rest on later academic reconstruction. The 1996 Machel study separately recorded children trafficked from Cambodia to brothels in Thailand. Child-specific findings against UNTAC personnel are not documented in the sources consulted.
cite: Wikipedia 'United Nations Transitional Authority in Cambodia' and 'Sexual abuse by UN peacekeepers'; Machel, Impact of Armed Conflict on Children, A/51/306 (1996)

n: AMISOM bases, Mogadishu — rape and sexual exploitation (HRW 2014)
who: African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) Ugandan and Burundian contingents
d: Human Rights Watch's 71-page report of 8 September 2014 documented AU soldiers on two Mogadishu bases raping women and girls as young as 12 and trading food aid for sex, including women seeking medicine for sick babies. The African Union rejected the findings as isolated cases.
cite: Human Rights Watch, 'The Power These Men Have Over Us', 8 September 2014, as summarised in Wikipedia 'African Union Mission to Somalia'

n: Afghanistan — bacha bazi by Afghan forces; US troops told not to intervene; SIGAR 2017
who: Afghan National Defense and Security Forces and Afghan Local Police commanders; US military chain of command
d: In 2011 a Kunduz mother reported that an Afghan Local Police commander had chained her 12-year-old son to a bed and raped him for two weeks; two US Special Forces soldiers who beat the commander were removed, later reinstated. The New York Times reported in September 2015 that US soldiers had been instructed by commanders to ignore child sexual abuse by Afghan allies. The Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction reported in June 2017 that DoD had 75 reports of gross human rights violations under review, 7 involving child sexual assault, and the NYT reported that aid was never cut off to an offending unit.
cover: NYT (2015) reported US soldiers were instructed not to intervene, in some cases even on US bases; US law (Leahy) required cutting aid to offending units but SIGAR/NYT reported that never happened. Capt. Dan Quinn was relieved and Sgt 1st Class Charles Martland initially separated after beating an ALP commander who admitted chaining and raping a 12-year-old boy (2011).
cite: SIGAR, Child Sexual Assault in Afghanistan: Implementation of the Leahy Laws (SIGAR 17-47-IP), June 2017 (not opened; figures via Wikipedia 'Bacha bazi'); NYT, 20 Sept 2015

n: China — Uyghur children separated from detained parents and placed in state boarding schools
who: Chinese state authorities in Xinjiang
d: Detention of Uyghur and other minority adults in Xinjiang left many children without parents; AP reported in September 2018 that thousands of boarding schools were being built, and the BBC and researcher Adrian Zenz reported in 2019 that children in them were penalised for not speaking Mandarin. Human Rights Watch said children were held at welfare facilities and boarding schools without parental consent. The New York Times reported about 497,000 pupils enrolled in December 2019. China denies the allegations. No sexual-abuse finding is recorded here; this is a child-removal record.
cite: Wikipedia 'Xinjiang internment camps' (citing AP Sept 2018, BBC 2019, HRW, NYT Dec 2019)

n: Okinawa — rape of a 12-year-old girl by three US servicemen (1995)
who: US Navy and Marine Corps personnel from Camp Hansen
d: On 4 September 1995 three US servicemen based at Camp Hansen abducted and raped a 12-year-old Okinawan girl. They were tried in a Japanese court under the US–Japan Status of Forces Agreement; in 1996 two were sentenced to seven years and one to six and a half years. The case triggered mass protests against the US bases.
cite: Wikipedia '1995 Okinawa rape incident'

n: Bosnia — Foča rape camps; ICTY Kunarac judgment (girls as young as 12 enslaved)
who: Bosnian Serb army (VRS) and paramilitaries; local police chief named in testimony
d: In Serb-held Foča, Bosniak women and girls, including minors as young as 12, were held in detention sites such as 'Karaman's house' and repeatedly raped. The ICTY convicted Dragoljub Kunarac (28 years' imprisonment for rape, torture and enslavement) and Radomir Kovač (20 years), who had raped a 12-year-old girl and then sold her into slavery; the Kunarac trial was the first conviction anywhere for using rape as a weapon of war. Witnesses identified the Foča police chief as visiting the camps to select women.
cite: ICTY, Prosecutor v. Kunarac, Kovač and Vuković (via Wikipedia 'Rape during the Bosnian War')

n: Chibok schoolgirls abduction — Boko Haram
who: Boko Haram (JAS)
d: On 14–15 April 2014 Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok, according to the local police; 57 escaped by jumping from the trucks, and the rest were believed taken to camps including the Sambisa Forest. Most later releases came via negotiated deals. Amnesty International said that on the tenth anniversary in April 2024, 82 girls remained in captivity, and estimated in 2015 that at least 2,000 women and girls had been abducted by the group since 2014, many forced into sexual slavery.
cite: Wikipedia 'Chibok schoolgirls kidnapping' (citing Amnesty International, 14 April 2024)

n: Dapchi schoolgirls abduction — ISWAP/Boko Haram
who: Boko Haram faction (ISWAP)
d: On 19 February 2018 militants abducted about 110 girls from a school in Dapchi. On 21 March 2018 the Nigerian government said 106 children, including 104 schoolgirls, had been returned; five girls died on the day of the abduction. One Christian girl, aged 14 at capture, who refused to convert, remained in captivity. An army intelligence document of 6 February 2018 had warned of a possible attack nearby.
cite: Wikipedia 'Dapchi schoolgirls kidnapping'

n: Kankara schoolboys abduction (Katsina, 2020)
who: Armed bandits; Boko Haram's Shekau claimed responsibility
d: On 11 December 2020 over 300 pupils were kidnapped from a boys' boarding school in Kankara. Boko Haram leader Abubakar Shekau claimed the abduction in an audio message; on 17 December the Katsina governor said 344 boys had been freed from a forest in Zamfara State.
cite: Wikipedia 'Kankara kidnapping'

n: LRA Makombo massacre and abductions, DR Congo (2009)
who: Lord's Resistance Army forces under Dominic Ongwen
d: In December 2009 LRA forces under Dominic Ongwen killed at least 321 civilians and abducted 250 people during a four-day attack in the Makombo area of north-eastern DR Congo. Between September 2008 and July 2011 the LRA abducted more than 3,000 people across DR Congo, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
cite: Wikipedia 'Lord's Resistance Army' (citing HRW reporting)

n: Colonia Dignidad (Chile) — child sexual abuse by Paul Schäfer; DINA detention and torture site
who: Colonia Dignidad sect led by Paul Schäfer; Chile's secret police DINA; West German embassy
d: German preacher Paul Schäfer, who left Germany in 1961 after accusations of molesting children, ran the colony, separating children from parents. Chile's National Commission for Truth and Reconciliation (Rettig, 1991) found evidence that the colony's land was used by DINA, Pinochet's secret police, for the detention and torture of political prisoners; former DINA agent Michael Townley confirmed the DINA link in 2005. A warrant was issued in 1996 after 26 children who attended the colony's school and clinic reported abuse; on 24 May 2006 Schäfer was sentenced to 20 years for 20 counts of indecent assault and 5 of forced sodomy against 25 minors between 1993 and 1997. He died in prison in 2010.
cover: In 1966 a teenager who fled took refuge at the West German embassy; the embassy sent a delegation and said it found no evidence. German diplomats praised it as a 'model colony'. Federal President Gauck said in July 2016 that German diplomats had for years looked away; Foreign Minister Steinmeier in April 2016 shortened the closure period of Foreign Office files from 30 to 20 years to release them. Schäfer fled in 1997 and was caught in Argentina in March 2005.
cite: Wikipedia 'Colonia Dignidad' and 'Paul Schäfer' (citing Rettig Commission 1991, Chilean court 2006); German Wikipedia 'Colonia Dignidad' (Steinmeier file release April 2016; Gauck July 2016; Bundestag resolution 29 June 2017)

n: Duplessis Orphans (Quebec) — healthy orphans falsely certified mentally ill and confined
who: Government of Quebec under Maurice Duplessis; Catholic religious orders running orphanages and hospitals
d: Under Premier Maurice Duplessis, many healthy children in Quebec orphanages were classified as mentally ill and sent to psychiatric hospitals because federal subsidies paid more for psychiatric patients ($2.75 a day) than orphans ($1.25); an early-1960s commission found one third of 22,000 patients were classified for financial reasons. Many survivors say they were physically and sexually abused and subjected to lobotomies, electroshock and straitjackets. Premier Lucien Bouchard apologised on 4 March 1999, and in 2001 Quebec offered about $25,000 per orphan, not covering sexual or other abuse. Claims linking the orphans to CIA MKUltra experiments are not established by the sources consulted.
cover: No criminal charges resulted from the 1990s complaints; the 2001 compensation excluded victims of sexual or other abuse.
cite: Wikipedia 'Duplessis Orphans' (citing CBC, 8 March 1999 and 1 July 2001)

n: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
d: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; about 1.2 million members, 4,000 of them paying. US IRS-CI traced Bitcoin payments and found the server in South Korea; the operator was arrested in March 2018. On 16 October 2019 US officials announced 337 arrests in 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). A US indictment sought extradition; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused it, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. Investigators said 45% of the site's videos had not been seen before.
cover: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Welcome to Video case' (citing BBC 16 Oct 2019 and 6 Jul 2020, Reuters 5 Jul 2022, Yonhap, Wired)

n: Freedom Hosting — Tor host for Lolita City and other abuse sites
who: Freedom Hosting (Eric Eoin Marques, convicted)
d: Freedom Hosting was the largest Tor web host by 2013 and hosted child-abuse sites including Lolita City (about 1.4 million images, 2013), which Anonymous had attacked and whose user list it leaked in 'Operation Darknet' in 2011. US agents obtained the server (hosted by OVH in France) by MLAT in July 2013 and the operator was arrested in Dublin on 1 August 2013 on a US warrant calling him 'the largest facilitator of child porn on the planet'. After the Irish Supreme Court dismissed his last appeal in March 2019 he was extradited, pleaded guilty in February 2020 to conspiracy to advertise child abuse images, and was sentenced to 27 years on 6 September 2021.
cover: Extradition from Ireland took from 2013 to 2019 through appeals.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Freedom Hosting' and 'Lolita City'

n: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
d: An invitation-only board whose members had to upload new material, with incentives for imagery of the abuse of children under 12. Servers were in Shreveport, Louisiana; top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 the US Attorney General announced 72 people charged and 52 arrested in 14 countries; by 2013, 57 had been arrested, 42 had pleaded guilty and sentences ranged from 10 years to life. Fifteen charged members were known only by online handles. DHS said up to 123 terabytes may have been distributed.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Operation Delego' (citing US DOJ releases)

n: Operation Torpedo — FBI ran three Tor sites
who: Three Tor-hidden abuse sites run by a Nebraska man
d: Dutch police compromised one site and found it physically hosted at a Nebraska web host; the FBI found an employee running two sites at work and one at home. After a year of surveillance the FBI arrested him and operated the sites for two weeks, using a network investigative technique to reveal visitors' IP addresses. The US DOJ said in December 2015 that 18 US users had been convicted besides the operator; one was the acting cybersecurity director of the US Department of Health and Human Services.
cover: The FBI kept the three sites running for two weeks from November 2012 and served a browser exploit to visitors.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Operation Torpedo' (citing US court filings and DOJ)

n: Childs Play — run by Australia's Task Force Argos for 11 months
who: Childs Play (Tor forum; owner Benjamin Faulkner, convicted)
d: Childs Play ran on Tor from April 2016 to September 2017 and was at its peak the largest site of its kind. US DHS arrested the Canadian owner in Virginia in October 2016; he and an associate were sentenced to life for the rape of a four-year-old and to 35 years for a child exploitation enterprise. Task Force Argos then ran the site until September 2017 as part of Operation Artemis, leading to further arrests and convictions, including a Canadian administrator sentenced to five years.
cover: Queensland Police Task Force Argos operated the site for about 11 months (2016–2017), impersonating the owner and posting abuse images to keep users' trust; a UNICEF Norway legal adviser and Amnesty International criticised this, ECPAT supported it, and a York University criminologist called the server move to Australia 'jurisdiction shopping'.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Childs Play (website)' (citing US DOJ, VG, CBC 'Hunting Warhead')

n: Nth Room and Doctor's Room — Telegram sexual blackmail rings
who: Telegram chatrooms 'Nth Room' (Moon Hyung-wook) and 'Doctor's Room' (Cho Ju-bin)
d: Operators blackmailed women and girls into producing sexual images and videos and sold access to Telegram rooms paid in cryptocurrency; content reached about 260,000 IDs (about 60,000 users after removing overlaps). The 'Doctor's Room' operator Cho Ju-bin was publicly named by police in March 2020 — the first such disclosure for a sex offender — and sentenced to 40 years on 26 November 2020 (reported raised to 42 years in October 2021). Moon Hyung-wook, creator of the original rooms, was sentenced to 34 years in 2021. Over five million people signed a petition to name buyers; the law was changed to punish possessing and viewing such material.
cover: A man's early 112 report was reportedly not treated as credible (Wikipedia, citation needed); two university students ('Team Flame') and journalists exposed it in 2019.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Nth Room case' (citing Yonhap, Hankyoreh, BBC)

n: South Korea school deepfake crisis on Telegram (2024)
who: Telegram group chats creating sexual deepfakes of classmates and teachers
d: In August 2024 investigations revealed Telegram groups where mostly teenage users made and shared sexual deepfakes of female classmates, teachers and relatives; the Korean Teachers Union estimated more than 200 schools were affected. South Korean police reported over 800 deepfake sex crime cases by end of September 2024, up from 156 in 2021, with most victims and offenders teenagers. On 26 September 2024 the National Assembly passed a bill criminalising possession or viewing of sexual deepfakes; police opened a probe into whether Telegram abetted the crimes.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Deepfake pornography' / 'Telegram deepfake scandal in South Korea' (citing Yonhap, Guardian, BBC)

n: AUSTRAC v Westpac — payments linked to child exploitation in the Philippines
who: Westpac Banking Corporation (failure to monitor transfers)
d: In November 2019 AUSTRAC alleged Westpac breached anti-money-laundering law 23 million times, covering $11 billion of transactions, including failures to properly vet transactions that could be linked to child exploitation and live child sex shows in the Philippines and south-east Asia. On 24 September 2020 Westpac and AUSTRAC agreed a A$1.3 billion penalty.
cite: Wikipedia, 'AUSTRAC' and 'Westpac' (citing AUSTRAC and Federal Court)

n: Australian man directed abuse of two children in the Philippines over Skype
who: Australian offender paying the children's mother
d: In 2016 Task Force Argos executed a warrant at a 58-year-old Australian man's home. Using Skype he conducted 'live remote' sexual abuse of two children in the Philippines, aged two and seven when it began, while paying their mother; it continued for nearly five years. He pleaded guilty to charges including having sex with a child under 16 outside Australia.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Cybersex trafficking' (citing Queensland Police / AFP)

n: Peter Scully — pay-per-view abuse streamed from Mindanao
who: 'No Limits Fun' dark web site (Peter Scully, Australian; Filipino accomplices)
d: An Australian who moved to the Philippines in 2011 ran a dark web site selling pay-per-view streams and videos of the torture and sexual abuse of children, procured with promises to poor parents. Dutch police opened the first investigation; he was arrested in Malaybalay on 20 February 2015. In June 2018 he was sentenced to life for the murder of a 12-year-old girl, human trafficking and five counts of rape; in November 2022 he got another 129 years. Accomplices who were themselves formerly trafficked were also prosecuted.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Peter Scully' (citing SMH, ABC, Philippine courts)

n: 'Sweetie' sting — 20,000 offers to pay for webcam abuse
who: Terre des hommes Netherlands (virtual 10-year-old 'Sweetie')
d: In a 10-week investigation from an Amsterdam warehouse, Terre des hommes used a computer-generated 'Filipino' girl to show the scale of webcam child sex tourism: 20,000 internet users offered to pay for webcam sex performances. About 1,000 were identified, in Australia, Canada, Jamaica, Germany, Ghana, India, Italy, Mauritius, the Netherlands, South Africa, Turkey, the UK and the US; 110 were in the UK and 254 traced to US computers.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Child sex tourism' (citing Terre des hommes)

n: Ogoshi brothers — Nigeria-based sextortion of a Michigan teenager
who: Samuel and Samson Ogoshi, Lagos (convicted); Ezekiel Ejehem Robert (charged)
d: Men in Lagos posed as a young woman on Instagram, obtained explicit images from a 17-year-old in Michigan and demanded money; he died by suicide on 25 March 2022. Indicted in May 2023, the brothers were arrested by Nigerian police and extradited in August 2023; prosecutors said they targeted hundreds of teenagers and adults in the US. They pleaded guilty in April 2024 and were each sentenced to 17.5 years on 4 September 2024; a third defendant contested extradition.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Death of Jordan DeMay' / 'Sextortion' (citing US DOJ W.D. Michigan, 10 April 2024; CBS)

n: 764 network — founder sentenced to 80 years
who: 764 (online network on Discord/Telegram; founder Bradley Cadenhead)
d: 764, named after the ZIP code prefix of Stephenville, Texas, extorted minors into producing abuse material, self-harm and animal cruelty. Its founder was arrested in August 2021 and in 2023 sentenced to 80 years after pleading guilty to possessing child sexual abuse material. The US DOJ describes 764 as a terror network; Canada (December 2025, the first country) and New Zealand list it as a terrorist entity. In April 2025 the DOJ announced arrests of two alleged leaders of a 764 subgroup, in North Carolina and in Greece. About 250 FBI investigations across all 55 field offices were reported in May 2025, and arrests in at least eight countries.
cite: Wikipedia, '764 (organization)' (citing US DOJ 29 Apr 2025, CBC 11 Dec 2025, Washington Post, Der Spiegel)

n: A.M. v. Omegle — site shut after child exploitation lawsuit
who: Omegle (random video chat)
d: A plaintiff known as A.M. from Oregon, sexually exploited as a child after being paired with an adult on Omegle, filed a $22 million lawsuit in 2019 alleging the site knowingly paired minors with predators. On 8 November 2023 the founder announced the site's closure; under an out-of-court settlement the final message thanked A.M. 'for opening my eyes to the human cost of Omegle' and linked the lawsuit.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Omegle' (citing BBC, court filings)

n: France charges Telegram founder Pavel Durov
who: Telegram (messaging platform)
d: Durov was arrested at Le Bourget on 24 August 2024 and on 28 August indicted on twelve charges, including complicity in the distribution of child sexual abuse material and drug trafficking; he was placed under judicial supervision. A BBC investigation in August 2024 found Telegram had not answered requests to join NCMEC or the IWF. On 4 December 2024 the IWF announced Telegram had joined and would use its hash lists to block known abuse imagery in public parts of the platform; the IWF said it had confirmed thousands of reports of abuse imagery on Telegram since 2022.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Arrest and indictment of Pavel Durov'; IWF news release, 4 December 2024

n: US state lawsuits against Roblox and Discord over child exploitation (alleged)
who: Roblox Corporation; Discord Inc.
d: Throughout 2025 state attorneys general sued Roblox alleging failures to protect children from predators: Louisiana (August), Kentucky (October), Texas (November), Iowa and Tennessee (December); Florida issued criminal subpoenas. In 2026 Nebraska and Los Angeles County sued, Indiana (May) and Arkansas (June) sued Roblox and Discord together, and Texas sued Discord. Roblox settled with Nevada ($10m+), Alabama and West Virginia (over $23m), Mississippi ($9m) and South Dakota ($8.6m), agreeing to age verification. These are allegations, not findings.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Roblox and child safety' and 'Discord' (citing state AG releases)

n: Apple cancels iCloud Photos CSAM scanning plan
who: Apple Inc.
d: Apple had scanned iCloud Mail for abuse imagery since 2019. On 5 August 2021 it confirmed plans to scan iCloud Photos; after public backlash over scanning on users' devices it paused and in December 2022 cancelled the plan.
cite: Wikipedia, 'iCloud' (citing Apple statements, Wired)

n: EU Child Sexual Abuse Regulation ('chat control') and interim derogation
who: European Commission, Council and Parliament
d: The Commission proposed the CSA Regulation (COM(2022) 209) to require platforms to assess risks and allow detection orders; it has been deadlocked over mandatory scanning. The interim derogation from the ePrivacy Directive (Regulation (EU) 2021/1232, in force 2 August 2021, extended in 2024) let providers voluntarily detect abuse material; with no agreement it lapsed on 3 April 2026. A new temporary derogation, Regulation (EU) 2026/1881, was adopted on 24 July 2026 and published 28 July 2026. As of October 2026 the permanent regulation has not been adopted.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Regulation to Prevent and Combat Child Sexual Abuse' (citing EUR-Lex, Council documents)

n: UK Online Safety Act 2023
who: UK Parliament / Ofcom
d: The Online Safety Act received royal assent on 26 October 2023, giving Ofcom powers over platforms' handling of illegal content including child sexual abuse material and content harmful to children. Many sites introduced age verification ahead of Ofcom's 25 July 2025 deadline.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Online Safety Act 2023'

n: US Kids Online Safety Act, EARN IT Act and REPORT Act
who: US Congress
d: The EARN IT Act, which would condition platforms' liability shield on child-safety practices, was introduced in 2020, 2022 and 2023 and died in committee. KOSA passed the Senate 91–3 on 30 July 2024, was reintroduced in May 2025, and in June 2026 the House Energy and Commerce Committee agreed an updated version without a 'duty of care', to be folded into the KIDS Act. The REPORT Act (2024) became law, requiring platforms to report online enticement and child sex trafficking to NCMEC; the TAKE IT DOWN Act took effect 19 May 2025.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Kids Online Safety Act', 'EARN IT Act', 'REPORT Act', 'TAKE IT DOWN Act'

n: Australia: eSafety Commissioner, Online Safety Act 2021 and under-16 social media ban
who: Office of the eSafety Commissioner
d: Australia enacted the Online Safety Act 2021 in June 2021, giving the eSafety Commissioner removal and transparency powers. In December 2024 parliament passed the Online Safety Amendment barring children under 16 from certain social media platforms; Roblox, initially excluded, was to be covered by protocols from March 2026. In June 2020 Australia also passed the Crimes Legislation Amendment (Sexual Crimes Against Children and Community Protection Measures) Act, which IJM said recognised Australians' role in demand for livestreamed abuse.
cite: Wikipedia, 'ESafety Commissioner'; 'Cybersex trafficking'

n: Stanford finds abuse material links in LAION-5B AI training dataset
who: LAION-5B dataset (German non-profit LAION)
d: In December 2023 the Stanford Internet Observatory reported 3,226 suspected links to child sexual abuse material in LAION-5B, a dataset used to train image generators, with 1,008 externally validated; the dataset was taken down. NCMEC's 2025 data counted more than 12,000 reports involving CSAM found in AI training data.
cite: Wikipedia, 'LAION'; NCMEC 'first look at 2025 data'

n: Grok image tool used to sexualise photos of minors (alleged)
who: X Corp / xAI (Grok)
d: In December 2025 users reported that X's Grok chatbot let people alter photos of real individuals, including minors, to show them undressed. In August 2026 a plaintiff ('Jane Doe') sued, alleging Grok was trained on abuse material of her and that the Canadian Centre for Child Protection had found Grok-generated AI CSAM depicting her. NCMEC listed X.AI among companies whose 2025 reports often lacked enough information to locate offences. These are allegations.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Grok (chatbot)'; NCMEC CyberTipline data 2025

n: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
d: Created in 1995 and run over encrypted internet chat, the club required members to supply 10,000 new images; members held more than 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, 1,500 officers in 13 countries arrested 104 suspects simultaneously on 2 September 1998. Of 1,263 children in the images, 17 were identified (UK 6, US 7, and one each in Argentina, Chile and Portugal).
cite: Wikipedia, 'Operation Cathedral' (citing BBC, Guardian)

n: Landslide Productions / Operations Avalanche and Ore
who: Landslide Productions (payment portal, Thomas and Janice Reedy)
d: A Texas portal that processed payments for websites including child abuse sites; the operators were convicted in August 2001. US Operation Avalanche made 100 arrests from 144 suspects; the FBI passed 7,272 UK names to British police, starting Operation Ore: 7,250 suspects, 3,744 arrests, 1,848 charged, 1,451 convictions and 140 children removed from danger. Follow-ups included Operation Snowball (Canada), Pecunia (Germany), Amethyst (Ireland), Genesis (Switzerland) and Auxin (Australia, ~200 arrests in 2004, including police officers and teachers). In total 390,000 people in over 60 countries were found to have accessed material.
cover: Later reconstruction of the Landslide data found many listed names were victims of credit-card fraud, and the validity of UK Operation Ore procedures was questioned; an estimated 33 suicides followed in the UK.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Operation Avalanche', 'Operation Ore', 'Operation Auxin'

n: Regpay — Minsk-based paid abuse sites / Operation Falcon
who: Regpay Co. Ltd (Belarus) with Florida payment firm Connections
d: A Minsk company ran about 50 paid websites selling access to child abuse images by credit card, with payments routed through Latvian banks. New Jersey prosecutors began Operation Falcon in 2003; Regpay's head and marketing director were detained in France on 30 July 2003 and its technical director extradited from Spain in 2004. All three confessed in US court and were sentenced to 25 years; the CEO of Connections pleaded guilty to money laundering.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Operation Falcon (child pornography investigation)'

n: Blue Orchid — Russian site selling abuse videos
who: Blue Orchid website
d: A website selling videos of the abuse of boys, mostly from Novokuybyshevsk, for about $300 each. A joint US Customs–Moscow City Police operation from May 2000 led to the arrest of four Americans and five Russians, including the site's creator.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Operation Blue Orchid'

n: LS Models / 'Alex Model' raids, Ukraine
who: 'Alex Model' agency (LS-Models brands)
d: A Kyiv modelling agency with branches in Kharkiv and Simferopol recruited children through TV, newspaper and radio adverts and produced sexualised images sold worldwide under 'LS' brands from 2001. Police raided it in July 2004; at the same time over 150 people were arrested in Australia for possession and distribution.
cover: Despite surveillance and arrests the legal outcome was described as lenient.
cite: Wikipedia, '2004 Ukrainian child pornography raids'

n: Austria-led 2007 investigation — 2,360 suspects in 77 countries
who: Online distribution network uncovered by Austrian authorities
d: Austrian authorities uncovered the network in July 2007 and investigated more than 2,360 suspects in 77 countries, about 600 in the US and 130 in Australia; Germany had the most European suspects.
cover: The two Irish suspects were not investigated by the Garda until six months after Austria notified them.
cite: Wikipedia, '2007 international child pornography investigation' (citing NBC News, 7 Feb 2007)

n: 'Kids the Light of our Lives' forum
who: Online chat forum with live streaming of abuse
d: A forum run from a farm in Suffolk hosting images and live streams of the abuse of children; the operator held 75,960 images and distributed up to 11,491. Acting on Virtual Global Taskforce information, a 10-month international operation arrested 700 men and rescued 31 children. The operator was convicted on 18 June 2007 at Ipswich Crown Court and given an indeterminate sentence.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Kids the Light of our Lives'

n: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
d: After complaints to cybertip.ca, Toronto police contacted the owner of Azov Films in October 2010 and raided it in May 2011; he allegedly earned over $4 million. Customer records were shared via the RCMP and Interpol across more than 50 countries; 348 people were arrested and 386 children said rescued when it was made public in November 2013. Primary producers were in Ukraine, Romania and Germany.
cover: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Project Spade' (citing Toronto Police, Globe and Mail, Spiegel)

n: Operation Blackwrist — Thai boys abused for Tor sites
who: Tor site administrators in Thailand and Australia
d: Interpol investigators in Asia found abuse material of children from Thailand on Tor sites in 2017; servers in Bulgaria were seized by Bulgarian cybercrime police. The main administrator in Thailand and another in Australia were arrested in early 2018; 11 boys under 13 were rescued in Thailand, about 50 children overall. Prosecutions followed in Thailand, Australia and the US (9 US arrests).
cite: Wikipedia, 'Operation Blackwrist'

n: Operation Lobos / Baby Heart (Brazil-led)
who: Baby Heart and other Tor boards
d: A Brazilian-centred, 12-country operation against the Tor board Baby Heart (online from 2015) and related sites, with the FBI and NCA. Two administrators were arrested in Portugal on 20 June 2017 and sentenced in January 2020; another administrator in Recife became an informant. The March–June 2019 phase led to 96 arrests.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Operation Lobos 1'

n: Bergisch Gladbach abuse complex
who: Chat groups of men sharing recordings of abuse of their own and other children
d: A house search in October 2019 found thousands of abuse images; the father had abused his daughter more than 60 times and shared recordings in chat groups. NRW's justice minister said in June 2020 that investigators had found 30,000 leads; by January 2022 the Cologne police unit had identified 439 suspects, reviewed over 130,000 photos and 12,000 videos and freed 65 children. The first suspect got 12 years plus preventive detention in October 2020; others got 14.5 and 13.5 years.
cite: German Wikipedia, 'Missbrauchskomplex Bergisch Gladbach' (citing WDR, Spiegel, NRW justice ministry)

n: Operación Roblox — extortion network in Panama
who: Network extorting minors through Roblox social features
d: In October 2024 Panamanian police, working with Spanish cybercrime intelligence, announced an operation to dismantle a network that produced abuse material by extorting minors through Roblox's social features.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Roblox and child safety' (citing La Prensa Panamá)

n: Gulf states block Roblox over child safety (2025)
who: Roblox Corporation
d: In August 2025 Roblox was banned in Qatar and Kuwait over child-safety concerns; Oman's telecoms regulator blocked it after reports of inappropriate content reaching minors, and Bahraini MPs drafted a ban. Palestine announced a ban in November 2025. Elsewhere, Kazakhstan's and Kyrgyzstan's authorities warned parents about predators, and Buenos Aires and three Argentine provinces blocked it on school devices after grooming reports.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Roblox and child safety'

n: Brazil orders Discord to suspend livestreaming (2026)
who: Discord Inc.
d: On 12 August 2026 the Brazilian government ordered Discord to block livestreaming in Brazil after a 13-year-old girl died by suicide having been encouraged to do so by others over a livestream; Brazil said Discord failed to meet its child-safety laws and threatened fines. Those involved were charged.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Discord' (citing Reuters)

n: Operation Hamlet — parents sharing abuse of their own children
who: International online network of offenders, many abusing their own children
d: Begun in November 2001 when Danish police, acting on a Save the Children tip, arrested a couple posting images of the abuse of their nine-year-old daughter. US Customs coordinated with Danish police, Interpol and NCMEC; by August 2002 about 10 people had been arrested in the US and 10 in Europe and 45 children rescued.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Operation Hamlet' (citing US Customs)

n: Operation Long Arm — 'Bamse' bulletin board (1992)
who: Bamse BBS (Danish bulletin board, ~900 users)
d: The first recorded US crackdown on internet child abuse material. A 1992 Miami arrest led to a Danish subscription bulletin board with up to 900 users in the US, Denmark and Australia; US Customs and Danish police made 34 arrests and convictions in the US and two in Australia. Start year approximate.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Operation Long Arm' (citing Akdeniz 2016)

n: Operation Soteria Shield (North Texas, 2025–2026)
who: FBI Dallas, North Texas ICAC Task Force, over 70 agencies, NCMEC
d: In April 2025 the operation arrested 244 suspects, rescued 109 children and seized 1,130 devices and 213 terabytes; in April 2026 it arrested 276 and rescued 89 children.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Operation Soteria Shield' (citing FBI Dallas)

n: Matthew Falder — dark web 'hurtcore' blackmailer
who: Individual offender posting on hurtcore dark web sites
d: A Birmingham university researcher posed as a woman online to coerce victims, many children, into sending degrading images, then used them as blackmail and posted them on hurtcore sites. The NCA, with GCHQ, US HSI, Europol and police in Australia, New Zealand and Israel, identified him after four years; he was arrested on 21 June 2017. He pleaded guilty to 137 charges and was jailed for 32 years in February 2018, reduced on appeal to 25 years.
cover: The NCA said technology companies' limited cooperation may have delayed identifying victims.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Matthew Falder' (citing NCA, BBC)

n: Spanish town: boys made AI nude images of 20 girls
who: Teenage boys using a 'nudify' website
d: In 2023 boys in a town in southern Spain used a 'nudify' website to make sexual deepfakes depicting at least 20 local girls aged 11 to 17.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Deepfake pornography'

n: Kik Messenger — groups distributing abuse material
who: Kik Messenger
d: In March 2016 the arrest of a registered sex offender uncovered more than 200 Kik groups dedicated to distributing and selling child abuse material. A UK police investigator said delays in getting information from the company increased risk to children. Kik joined the Virtual Global Taskforce in 2015 and added image-detection in October 2016.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Kik Messenger'

n: Operation Protect Our Children — domain seizures (2011)
who: US ICE HSI
d: In February 2011 ICE and the DOJ seized 10 domain names advertising and distributing child abuse material. One seized domain belonged to a shared DNS provider, so all 84,000 of its subdomains, mostly unrelated, briefly displayed the seizure notice.
cover: Seizure of one shared domain redirected about 84,000 unrelated subdomains to a seizure warning.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Operation Protect Our Children'
